content.content:
## sam-3.1

- **What it does:** Segments images and video. Give it a short noun phrase (for example, "yellow school bus") and it returns every match.
- **Image segmentation:** Yes. Matches are returned as boxes and pixel-accurate masks.
- **Video object tracking:** Yes. The page says it follows each object across frames, but doesn't describe the track output format.
- **Prompts:** Text noun phrases, plus boxes and points to segment specific objects.
- **Returns:** Boxes and masks. The page doesn't mention a separate tracks field.
- **Input/output:** Text prompt, image, or video in; boxes and masks out.
- **Limits and parameters:** Not stated on the page.
- **Endpoint:** `POST /v1/responses` (Responses API). Upload clips via the Files API if you segment them more than once.
- **Docs:** [Models](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/models#sam-3), [Media segmentation guide](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/media-segmentation), [Responses API](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/protocols/responses), [Create response](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/api-reference/responses/create-response), [File handling](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/file-handling)

## muse-image-1.0

- **What it does:** Generates images from a text prompt (with optional reference images) and edits images from an instruction. It can search the web for references and run code to build layouts first.
- **Input/output:** Text and image in; image out.
- **Limits and parameters:** Not stated on the page.
- **Endpoints:**
  - Responses API, for multi-turn editing
  - `/v1/images/generations`, for one-off generation
  - `/v1/images/edits`, for one-off editing
- **Docs:** [Models](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/models#muse-image), [Image generation guide](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/image-generation), [Create image](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/api-reference/images/create-image), [Edit image](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/api-reference/images/edit-image)

## muse-wonder-1.0

- **What it does:** Meta's most capable model, for complex software engineering and long-horizon agentic work. Supports computer use, tool calling, structured output, and search grounding.
- **Input/output:** Text, image, video, audio, and PDF in; text out.
- **Limits:** 1,048,576-token context window. Preview status.
- **Reasoning effort:** Levels from `"minimal"` to `"max"`. The page doesn't give the request field name.
- **Endpoints:** Responses, Chat Completions, and Messages (the page lists these for Muse Wonder and Muse Spark together).
- **Availability:** Model API pay-as-you-go in Standard mode only. Not available in South Korea.
- **Docs:** [Models](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/models#muse-wonder), [Model page](https://dev.meta.ai/models/muse-wonder), [Model card](https://research.meta.ai/static/muse-wonder-model-card), [Reasoning](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/reasoning), [Chat Completions](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/protocols/chat-completions)

## muse-spark-1.3

- **What it does:** Meta's model for agentic and coding work. The page recommends it for new work.
- **Input/output:** Text, image, video, audio, and PDF in; text out.
- **Limits:** 1,048,576-token context window.
- **Reasoning effort:** All levels, including `"max"`.
- **Audio caveat:** Audio understanding isn't fully supported in 1.3. Use 1.2 for audio requests.
- **Endpoints:** Responses, Chat Completions, and Messages.
- **Availability:** Model API pay-as-you-go in Standard mode.
- **Docs:** [Models](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/models#muse-spark), [Pricing and rate limits](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/pricing-rate-limits), [Chat Completions](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/protocols/chat-completions)

## Contributor variants

- **`muse-spark-1.3-contributor`** and **`muse-spark-1.2-contributor`**
- **Mode:** Contributor mode, at a lower price. Your content may be used to train future Meta models.
- **Limits:** The page gives no separate limits. The 1.3 contributor variant doesn't support `"max"` reasoning effort.
- **Endpoints:** Same as the Muse Spark models they correspond to.
- **Docs:** [Models](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/models#muse-spark), [Pricing and rate limits](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/pricing-rate-limits#contributor-mode)

## muse-voice-transcribe-1.0

- **What it does:** Speech-to-text for live audio streams and supported audio files. Supports streaming speaker diarization, voice activity detection, keyword biasing, and turn-level timestamps. Covers 25 evaluated languages.
- **Input/output:** Audio in; text transcript out.
- **Not supported:** Speech synthesis, speech-to-speech, word-level timestamps, sound event detection, and emotion detection.
- **Limits:** Not stated beyond the language count.
- **Endpoints:**
  - `wss://api.meta.ai/v1/asr/realtime`, for live audio
  - `POST /v1/asr/transcribe`, for files
- **Docs:** [Models](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/models#muse-voice-transcribe), [Speech-to-text guide](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/speech-to-text), [Transcribe](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/api-reference/voice/transcribe), [Audio pricing](https://dev.meta.ai/docs/pricing-rate-limits#muse-voice-transcribe-pricing)

The source doesn't include a video request example, only a note that clips attach through an `input_video` part. The full image request and response exceed the 125-character quote limit, so I can't quote them whole. Instead, I've quoted the key lines and described the rest.

## Image request

The request goes to `POST /v1/responses` on `https://api.meta.ai/v1`, with the `sam-3.1` model and streaming enabled. The main lines are:

- `baseURL: "https://api.meta.ai/v1",`
- `model: "sam-3.1",`
- `{ type: "input_text", text: "yellow school bus" },`
- `{ type: "input_image", image_url: "https://example.com/street.png" },`
- `stream: true,`

The body is one user message containing a short noun phrase and one image part. The parser example also adds `metadata: { mask_encoding: "one_bit" }` so masks come back as binary rasters.

## Video request

No video example appears in the source. Video goes in an `input_video` part, using the same message structure as the image request. The source recommends streaming for video so each frame renders as it is segmented.

## Example response

The full response is one long line that exceeds the quote limit, so here is its structure:

- **Frame marker:** `<0f>` identifies the frame. Video responses have one line per frame.
- **Object ordinal:** a leading integer (`0`, then `1` for the second object) identifies each object.
- **Box token=*** `<|box;...|>` follows the object's ordinal.
- **Mask token=*** `<|mask;...|>` follows the box.

A representative fragment begins: `<0f>0<|box;x1=353;y1=382;x2=453;y2=427;w=537;h=561|><|mask;x=0;y=0;data=46,101,~...|>`. The source truncates mask payloads with `~...`, and `~` marks a lossless mask payload.

## Parsing boxes

- Boxes arrive in source pixels.
- `x1`, `y1`, `x2`, and `y2` give the box corners.
- `w` and `h` give the dimensions of the reference image. The source doesn't define them explicitly, so confirm this in the grammar documentation.

## Parsing masks

- Each mask carries `x` and `y` offsets and a `data` payload.
- Use `@meta-sam/parser` rather than parsing the grammar by hand. Pass the stream to `parseImageStream`, read `finalResult`, and filter records with `recordsOfKind(..., "mask")`.
- `decodeMaskToRaster` converts a mask into a `Uint8Array` of 0s and 1s with length `W * H`.
- Set `mask_encoding` to `one_bit` in metadata to get binary rasters. The source mentions other encodings but doesn't describe them here.

## Limits

- **Prompts:** use a short noun phrase naming one concrete object. Send separate requests for multiple object types. Use box and point prompts for objects you've already located.
- **Video formats:** MP4 and MOV containers encoded with H.264, H.265, or MPEG-4.
- **Zero matches:** the stream completes with empty `output_text`, so your code must handle that case.
- **Identity:** objects keep stable identities across frames.
- **Not specified:** file size, frame count, resolution, and rate limits aren't covered in the source.

content.text:
Not as raw output. SAM's response can't go straight into json-render, but it can be the input to a step that produces a json-render spec:

- **What SAM returns:** a stream of special tokens (`<0f>0<|box;x1=…|><|mask;…|>`), meaning which object, where it is, and its pixel mask. It doesn't say what the element is beyond your prompt word, and it doesn't read the text on it.
- **What json-render needs:** a spec made only of catalog components (`button`, `table`, `input`…) with their props, validated against the catalog before rendering. A raw feed would bypass that validation, which the rules forbid.

So the pipeline needs three pieces, with a clear job each:

| Step | Who | Produces |
|---|---|---|
| **Where** | SAM 3.1, one call per element type ("button", "table", "text input", "tab") | boxes and masks |
| **What** | Muse Spark (it reads images), given each cropped region | the element's text, label and role, e.g. "button: Refresh" |
| **Map and validate** | Code | a json-render spec: each detection becomes a catalog component, placed by its box, then validated against the catalog |

Following the "judgments from the model, decisions in code" rule: SAM and Spark observe, and code decides which component each detection becomes, so an invalid or unknown element can't slip through.

This also fits your dev cycle: segmentation could be a sealed method whose results arrive as a schema feed, so the UI receives detections like any other plugin's state and turns them into a validated spec.

Should I write this up as a short spec in `docs/` for omp? I'd include the SAM output parsing, the Spark labelling call, the component mapping table and validation, and use the 46 old dashboard screenshots as the test set.

content.text:
Yes. SAM 3.1 takes a text prompt, and that makes the link with json-render direct. The catalog's own component names can be the prompts:

```
json-render catalog          SAM 3.1 (text prompt + image)      code
──────────────────           ─────────────────────────────      ──────────────────────────────
"button"          ───────▶   boxes + masks of every button ───▶ each match → a `button` element
"table"           ───────▶   boxes + masks of every table  ───▶ each match → a `table` element
"text input" …    ───────▶   …                              ───▶ … → spec, validated against the catalog
```

So the catalog drives the detection:
- **Input:** for each component the catalog declares, send its name, or a short noun phrase from its description, as SAM's text prompt with the screenshot. Only things the catalog knows how to render are looked for.
- **Output:** SAM's reply is text too, the special-token stream (`<0f>0<|box;…|><|mask;…|>`). A small parser turns it into records of object, box and mask.
- **Spec:** code turns each record into that same catalog component, positioned by its box, and json-render validates the spec before rendering.

One limit from Meta's docs: one short noun phrase per request, so it's one call per component type per screenshot. Muse Spark can then fill in what SAM can't, the text on each element, from the cropped region.

The result: screenshot plus catalog gives a validated json-render spec, with no hand-written mapping of what to look for. Should I write this up as the spec for omp?
